en: Vimānavatthu:
Purisavimāna,
Mahārathavagga
2. The Story of the Mansion of Revatī “A man who has lived abroad for a long time,
having returned safely from afar;”
Relatives, friends, and dear companions rejoice at one's arrival;
even so do those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Having passed away from this world,
merits receive him just as beloved kinsmen welcome a returning friend.
“Arise, Revatī, you of evil character!
You who have left the door open and are of a nature not to give—
let us lead you away to where those who fare ill are being praised!”
"Afflicted with suffering are those in hell.
Having spoken thus, those two great red-eyed yakkhas, the messengers of Yama, departed.
Taking Revata by his arms,
they led him away into the presence of the host of gods:
“He is of sun-like color, beautiful and radiant.”
"Whose is this celestial mansion, bright and covered with a golden lattice,
filled with people and shining like the rays of the sun?"
Multitudes of women, anointed with the essence of sandalwood,
adorn the celestial mansion on both sides;
it appears there, possessing a color equal to the sun.
"Who rejoices, having reached heaven in a celestial palace?
"In Benares there was one named Nandiya,
a lay follower, free from stinginess, a lord of giving, and generous."
That celestial mansion,
crowded with people and shining like the rays of the sun,
was filled with throngs of women anointed with the essence of sandalwood.
They adorn the celestial mansion on both sides;
it appears with a color equal to the sun,
and having reached heaven, he rejoices in that mansion.
“I am the wife of Nandiya,
a householder and mistress of the entire household;
I shall delight in my husband’s celestial mansion, and I shall give gifts.”
“Do not long to see hell.
“This is your hell, O you of evil nature;
no merit has been performed by you in the world of the living.”
"For one who is stingy, irascible,
and of evil character does not attain companionship with those who go to heaven.
"What indeed is feces and urine?"
"It appears impure;
what is this foul-smelling filth?
What is it that exudes?"
“This is the one called Saṃsāvaka,
profound and a man of truth;
wherein for thousands of years— ”
“Then you yourself must cook it, Revatī.
“What misdeed have I committed by body, speech, or mind?”
“By whom was such a companion found,
so profound and a man among sages?
“Both among recluses and brahmins...”
Or even other mendicants;
you deceived them with false speech—
this evil was committed by you.
By that he obtained a dwelling,
deep and a hundred men in height;
there, for thousands of years,
You are roasted, Revatī;
they cut off your hands and also your feet,
they cut off your ears and also your nose.
"Then flocks of crows and owls,
having gathered and assembled together, devour me as I writhe.
"It would be well indeed if you would lead me back."
I shall perform much wholesome merit:
through generosity, through even conduct,
and through restraint and self-control.
“Having done which they become happy and do not regret it later.
“In the past you were heedless;”
Now you lament;
you shall experience the ripening of the deeds you yourself have done.
“Who, having gone from the world of the gods to the world of men,
when asked by me, would speak thus:
‘Give gifts to those who have laid down the rod’?”
“Clothing, bedding, food, and drink— indeed,
one who is miserly, irascible,
and of evil character does not attain companionship with those who go to heaven.”
Having surely gone from here and obtained a human birth,
may I be generous and endowed with virtue.
I shall perform much wholesome merit:
through generosity, through even conduct,
and through self-restraint and self-mastery.
I shall plant groves and causeways on difficult paths,
as well as ponds and wells.
With a serene mind,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth,
and on the eighth day of the fortnight;
And on the fortnight of miracles,
I shall observe the Uposatha day, perfectly endowed with its eight factors.
Always restrained in moral conduct,
I shall not be negligent in generosity;
this has been seen by me for myself.
As she was thus lamenting and writhing here and there,
they hurled her into a terrible hell.
With feet upturned and head hanging down:
"In the past, I was miserly,
reviling ascetics and brahmins."
"And having deceived my husband with falsehood,
I am now burning in a hell of terrible form.
Thus ends the second *Revatī-vimāna*.
